She has spent more than 12 years in fintech and payments across North America and Europe, including nine years at OFX in partnerships and solutions engineering before joining Stripe as an implementation consultant. Since co-founding Yeeld in 2022 she has led the company’s product strategy and development, and oversees its commercial and operational functions. She spoke at Stripe Sessions 2026, is a judge for the PayTech Awards USA, and earned her MBA from UCLA Anderson’s part-time programme. British-Canadian and originally from Darlington, she now lives in Seattle.

title: Intermex sues Western Union
snippet: The long-time remittance provider walked away from a $500 million merger deal due to “buyer’s remorse,” Intermex alleged in a Tuesday lawsuit.
fullText:
Dive Brief:

International Money Express sued Western Union on Tuesday seeking to enforce the terms of its $500 million merger agreement that Western Union abandoned earlier this month. Western Union contracted “a bad case of buyer’s remorse” over the 2025 deal as the remittance business deteriorated, according to the lawsuit.

Western Union gained at least $50 million in annual cost savings and financial improvements by studying Intermex’s operations during the merger planning period, according to the lawsuit. “By walking away, Western Union got that value at the expense of Intermex’s stockholders without having to pay those stockholders a dime,” Intermex said in the lawsuit filed in Delaware.

Western Union “stands by its decision to terminate the merger agreement and strongly disagrees with the claims asserted by Intermex in its lawsuit,” a spokesperson said Tuesday in an email. “We believe we acted in accordance with the terms of the merger agreement and intend to vigorously defend against the lawsuit.”

Dive Insight:

The lawsuit filed in the Delaware Court of Chancery alleges breach of contract by Western Union for not completing the deal, and seeks to enforce the merger agreement, along with injunctive relief and damages.

“Intermex believes Western Union’s purported termination is invalid given that all conditions to the closing have been satisfied,” the company said Tuesday in a press release.

The merger deal dates to August 2025, when Western Union agreed to pay $16 per share for Miami-based Intermex, which was founded in 1994 and enables money transfers from the U.S. and four other countries to about 60 nations, with a network of thousands of bank and retail locations.

Denver-based Western Union, which provides cross-border payments services and has roots reaching back more than 100 years, provides remittance services at locations worldwide.

On Aug. 14, the California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation – which had earlier approved the transaction – suspended an approval it had granted only two weeks before. That decision occurred the same day New York regulators approved the merger, with conditions.

Intermex said Western Union “seized” on the August California DFPI decision “as an opportunity to escape the deal and abscond with hundreds of millions of dollars in synergies, while leaving Intermex a wounded company,” according to the lawsuit. “Rather than using its reasonable best efforts to fix the problem in California, Western Union sat on its hands and let the clock run.”

The company had “insisted on control of the regulatory process,” Intermex said in the lawsuit, but failed to engage in constructive talks with the California agency, which is led by Rohit Chopra, the former director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. The DFPI approved the merger, with conditions, on Nov. 10. 

“Western Union deliberately stalled, offering nothing and leaving it to DFPI to propose conditions on its own, knowing that every day of delay brought it closer” to the Nov. 10 date, which permitted termination of the agreement if the deal had not closed.

However, Western Union CEO Devin McGranahan “met privately with Secretary Chopra, without Intermex, in discussions that, upon information and belief, addressed whether the $16 price was too high,” Intermex said in the lawsuit.

McGranahan also held a town hall meeting on Oct. 13 with Intermex employees and said the Nov. 10 closing date would be extended if necessary, according to the lawsuit.

The remittance business has been turbulent over the past two years amid U.S. changes in immigration policies under the Trump administration, plus the longer-running industry shift from physical money-remittance stores to digital channels.

Last year, remittances to Mexico – the largest remittance recipient in the Americas – fell for the first time in 11 years, declining about 4% to $62.5 billion, according to the lawsuit.

These changes were caused by reduced migrant workers in the U.S., “which multiple industry analysts have attributed as a significant factor in declining remittances,” Intermex said in the suit. Intermex also cited a 1% excise tax on remittances the U.S.  imposed on Jan. 1, along with the industry move from retail to digital channels.

“Western Union came under intense pressure from its stockholders to find a way to escape from the deal it had agreed to a year earlier,” the lawsuit said.

title: OCI Shareholders Approve Orascom Construction Combination at EGM
snippet: OCI N.V. shareholders have backed all resolutions for the Orascom Construction merger, with delisting from Euronext Amsterdam set for 27 November 2026. The post OCI Shareholders Approve Orascom Construction Combination at EGM appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
OCI N.V., the Amsterdam-listed fertiliser and chemicals group, has secured unanimous shareholder approval at an Extraordinary General Meeting for its proposed business combination with Orascom Construction PLC. Every resolution put to the vote passed, including those relating to the combination itself and the OCIN Sale, with minority shareholders providing majority support on each item.

The vote sets in motion a tightly sequenced series of corporate and settlement steps running through the end of 2026 and into the first half of 2027.

Key dates and mechanics

Euronext Amsterdam has confirmed the delisting of OCI shares effective 27 November 2026, making 26 November the final day on which the stock will trade with entitlement to the distribution of Orascom Construction shares. The demerger deed, the outstanding corporate step needed to make the demerger effective, is expected to be executed on or around 2 November 2026; OCI received confirmation from the Amsterdam District Court on 20 October that no creditor had filed an objection against the demerger.

Shareholders wishing to tender their OCI shares under the voluntary offer made by NNS have until 17 November 2026 at 17:40 CET, though OCI has emphasised that individual intermediaries may impose earlier instruction deadlines and shareholders should contact their bank, broker or custodian promptly.

The record date for the distribution of Orascom Construction shares is currently expected to fall on 30 November 2026, subject to the timetable for any Post-Closing Acceptance Period and its settlement. Crediting of Orascom Construction shares to eligible shareholder accounts is targeted to commence on or around 8 December 2026, though OCI cautioned that individual receipt dates may vary significantly depending on intermediary processes and the completeness of settlement information provided. Dissolution and liquidation of OCI itself is expected to commence between December 2026 and the first half of 2027.

On the tax side, OCI will sell a portion of Orascom Construction shares to fund Dutch dividend withholding tax obligations linked to the distribution. The number of shares sold will be calibrated to the applicable withholding percentage, and OCI confirmed that any shortfall in sale proceeds will be funded for the account of the combined company rather than charged back to shareholders through additional share withholding.

Regulatory and market context

The combination represents a significant restructuring of OCI’s listed footprint in Europe. Delistings of this kind from Euronext Amsterdam require coordinated approvals from the exchange, Dutch corporate courts and, where relevant, securities regulators in other jurisdictions in which the issuer operates. The Amsterdam District Court’s confirmation that no creditor objected to the demerger removes a potential procedural delay, though the overall timetable remains explicitly indicative and subject to the pace of NNS’s offer process.

For institutional shareholders holding OCI through custodian chains, the settlement mechanics are the operationally critical variable. Distributed share entitlements in cross-border demerger structures frequently experience timing dispersion across intermediaries, particularly where beneficial ownership sits across multiple settlement systems. OCI’s decision to address suspense arrangements explicitly in the EGM circular suggests the company is alive to that operational risk.

The combination consolidates OCI’s industrial construction assets into a single listed Orascom Construction vehicle, a structural simplification that mirrors a broader trend among diversified holding companies on European exchanges seeking to reduce discount-to-NAV pressure by eliminating conglomerate complexity.

title: Bill sells for $6B to TPG, Corpay
snippet: The deal for the bill-pay company fuels consolidation in the business payments and receivables software industry.
fullText:
Bill Holdings will go private in a $6 billion cash takeout announced Thursday, with investment firm TPG and corporate payments player Corpay acquiring the billing and payments finance software firm.

TPG is acquiring the majority share of Bill, with Corpay paying $1.1 billion for a 33% stake of the company and an option to acquire the full company by 2030.

The Bill deal marks a reprisal of TPG and Corpay’s playbook for their $2.2 billion purchase last year of business payments firm AvidXchange, with Corpay buying 34% of Avid for $550 million and the same option for a 100% ownership stake.

Bill, based in San Jose, California, provides software services to small and midsize companies to help handle payment, invoicing, accounts receivable, spending and expense management and other functions.  

“This transaction marks an exciting new chapter for Bill, delivering significant, certain, and immediate value to our stockholders, while creating new opportunities to accelerate our transformation and deliver greater value to customers,” René Lacerte, who founded the company in 2006 and serves as CEO, said in a press release Thursday.

Lacerte will continue as Bill CEO after the sale closes, the company said.

“Given our successful relationship with TPG, we are excited to participate in this transaction and invest in another large, complementary corporate payments business,” Corpay Chairman and CEO Ron Clarke said in a Thursday press release.

Lacerte has spent more than a year aiming to reorganize the company and boost profits after adding four new directors last year under pressure from activist investors. 

Hedge funds Starboard Value and Elliott Investment Management acquired large stakes in Bill last year, seeing the potential for more robust profits with changes at the company.

Bill added a slate of new executives this year and has integrated an array of new artificial intelligence tools to speed product introductions and boost efficiencies. Bill has also cut jobs to help financial performance.

In December, a third Bill investor, Barington Capital Group, called on Bill to consider a sale, arguing that public markets were unwilling “to assign a fair valuation” for the company. A Barington executive declined to comment Friday.

Bill has “long recognized the significant opportunity at the intersection of financial technology, AI, and payments,” TPG Partner John Flynn said in the release. The company is “well positioned to capitalize on these trends through its scaled network, integrated technology, and deep customer relationships,” he added.

TPG and Atlanta-based Corpay will pay $63.25 per share in cash for Bill, which the companies said was a 31% premium to the 60-day average share price on Nov. 16, the day before the Financial Times reported that TPG was nearing a deal for Bill.

The deal is expected to close the first half of next year. Bill’s largest shareholder, Starboard Value, and Lacerte have agreed to vote their shares for the acquisition, Bill said in its press release. Together, they own about 11.1% of Bill shares, the company said Friday in a regulatory filing.

Corpay is likely to absorb both AvidXChange and Bill, with the latter deal occurring once Bill reaches organic revenue growth in the mid-teens and profit margins above 50%, William Blair analyst Andrew Jeffrey wrote Friday in a note to clients.

The TPG-Corpay acquisition of AvidXChange closed in October 2025.

“Bill’s back-office technology assets were clearly highly complementary to both Avid and Corpay’s core spend management portfolio,” Jeffrey wrote, with “significant long-term synergies” despite differing customer segments.

Bill was “clearly an attractive price” for Corpay, said Jeffrey, who had expected Bill to fetch a share price in the mid-$70s range.

“We like the prospects of a more scaled corporate payments and spend management business, though we think some of this potential upside is likely being reflected” in Corpay’s current stock price, Jeffrey wrote. He also predicted that Corpay would sell its lodging segment, which helps companies with negotiated hotel rates and integrated billing and payment tools.

Starboard and Elliott did not respond to messages this week about Bill’s potential sale.

title: Moving Money in an AI World: Are We Adapting to the Hype or Building for What’s Next?
snippet: Fintechs are looking beyond single products, using AI, stablecoins and integrated financial infrastructure to expand services, streamline operations and support global business growth. The post Moving Money in an AI World: Are We Adapting to the Hype or Building for What’s Next? appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
There is a lot happening in fintech. AI is changing how quickly companies can build products, stablecoins are creating new ways to move money globally, and financial services businesses are thinking about how much of their operations can be automated.

But I keep coming back to a more basic question: are we building businesses around genuine opportunities, or are we getting carried away with the latest technology hype?

For years, fintech founders were encouraged to focus. Find a problem, build one product, establish yourself in a market and expand from there. Trying to do too much across too many markets was generally seen as a distraction.

But perhaps that thinking needs revisiting.

Consider Revolut. Founder and CEO Nik Storonsky has spoken about the company’s approach to launching new products. Rather than relying purely on intuition, Revolut gives small, dedicated teams the opportunity to test new ideas, measures their performance through gross profit growth and scales the products that demonstrate traction. Those that don’t perform are discontinued.

I find this approach interesting because it challenges the idea that fintechs should necessarily stick to one product. It isn’t about launching everything and hoping something works. It’s about having the ability to experiment, identify opportunities and allocate resources accordingly.

AI makes this even more relevant. If the time and cost involved in building software continue to fall, launching new products becomes easier. But that doesn’t mean finding customers, entering new markets or making money becomes any easier.

And this is where the next generation of fintech businesses gets interesting.

Stripe: Making Global Money Movement Easier

Stripe is a good example of how the opportunity is expanding beyond traditional payments.

The company has been building out its financial infrastructure across payments, Treasury, stablecoins, crypto and global money movement. It is increasingly positioning itself as infrastructure for businesses that need to operate internationally without having to piece together multiple financial providers.

In a conversation with Neetika Bansal, Stripe’s Head of Money Management and Crypto, an interesting problem emerged.

Businesses, particularly AI companies, can operate across dozens or even hundreds of markets from day one. They can acquire customers globally without necessarily having a physical presence in every country. But managing the money that comes with that growth is another matter.

Multi-currency balances, international payments, card issuing and currency conversions can still involve fragmented financial applications and complicated integrations.

Stripe Treasury and its wider financial infrastructure are designed to make this easier, giving businesses access to financial accounts, balances, cards and money movement through a more unified experience.

Stablecoins and crypto infrastructure are becoming an increasingly important part of that proposition.

What I find particularly interesting is that the end customer doesn’t necessarily need to know crypto is involved. Stripe is effectively trying to remove the complexity, providing the wallet infrastructure, card infrastructure and orchestration through APIs.

The objective isn’t necessarily to get businesses or consumers excited about blockchain. It’s to make moving money easier.

Is the Dollar Becoming More Digital?

There is another interesting dimension to Stripe’s strategy: the role of the US dollar in global payments.

Dollar-backed stablecoins are creating another way to hold and transfer value across borders. For businesses operating internationally, they could offer faster settlement and access to dollar-based financial infrastructure without relying entirely on traditional banking channels.

Meta‘s use of Stripe’s stablecoin infrastructure to pay creators in Colombia and the Philippines is a practical example.

Rather than making creators navigate the complexities of blockchain, the idea is to allow them to receive USDC through compatible wallets and access their funds through familiar financial services.

This is where I think the stablecoin opportunity becomes more interesting. It isn’t necessarily about replacing traditional banking or persuading everyone to hold crypto. It’s about making the underlying infrastructure more efficient.

And if businesses can access global financial services through a single integration, that changes the economics of international expansion.

Who Takes Responsibility When AI Starts Moving Money?

Of course, making money easier to move creates another question, particularly as AI agents become more involved in financial transactions.

We’ve already spent considerable time discussing agentic payments and the question of who controls the transaction. But there is another side to this: who is responsible when something goes wrong?

If an AI agent can make purchases, initiate payments or move money on behalf of a business, how do we establish that it has the authority to do so?

What happens if it makes an incorrect payment, is manipulated or acts outside the permissions it was given?

Banks and payment providers already have significant responsibilities around fraud, identity verification and transaction monitoring. Introducing agents into the equation makes those responsibilities more complicated.

This is where companies such as GrailPay are worth watching.

GrailPay is positioning its risk intelligence platform as an authorization layer for faster bank payments and the emerging world of agentic commerce.

The proposition is interesting because the industry needs more than the ability to execute transactions. It needs to understand the risk behind them, establish who is authorising them and determine whether they should be allowed to proceed.

As payments become increasingly automated, authorization and risk intelligence could become just as important as the payment rails themselves.

But the liability question still needs answering. Banks, payment providers and technology companies will all have a role to play, and someone will ultimately need to take responsibility.

Mercury: More Than Just a Business Bank Account

Another company I find interesting is Mercury.

Mercury started by making banking better for startups and businesses. But its ambition has moved beyond offering a business bank account.

It is building what increasingly looks like a financial operating system, bringing together banking, cards, payments, treasury management and financial workflows.

Its introduction of Mercury Command also points towards how AI could change the way businesses interact with their finances.

Rather than navigating different dashboards, reviewing transactions and managing everything manually, businesses can increasingly use AI to interact with their financial information and automate parts of their operations.

I think this is an important development because the opportunity isn’t simply to add an AI chatbot to a banking app. It’s to change how businesses manage money altogether.

But there is a distinction between making financial operations easier and giving AI greater control over them.

Permissions, security, auditability and human oversight still matter. Particularly when you’re dealing with business finances.

Mercury’s direction raises an interesting question: will the next generation of successful fintechs look less like banks and more like operating systems for businesses?

What Happens to Compliance?

There is another area I think deserves more attention: regulatory compliance.

Financial services have always been expensive to build and operate. Compliance teams, customer onboarding, transaction monitoring, fraud prevention and regulatory reporting all require significant resources.

AI could fundamentally change the economics of these activities.

Many compliance processes involve reviewing large amounts of information, identifying unusual patterns and carrying out repetitive checks. AI could make much of this work faster and potentially reduce the operational costs involved.

For smaller fintechs, that could be particularly significant. If the cost of managing compliance falls, building and scaling a regulated financial services business could become more accessible.

But I wouldn’t underestimate the challenge.

Automating compliance doesn’t remove regulatory responsibility. Financial institutions still need to understand how decisions are being made, demonstrate appropriate oversight and remain accountable when something goes wrong.

The opportunity is there, but the question is how much of the regulatory burden can genuinely be automated without introducing new risks.

So, Should Fintechs Build More or Focus?

Looking at Revolut, Stripe, GrailPay and Mercury, there is a common theme.

They are approaching financial services from different directions, but each is looking beyond a single financial product. Whether it’s global money movement, risk intelligence, business banking or financial automation, the opportunity increasingly sits in connecting different parts of the financial system.

But that doesn’t mean every fintech should try to become a financial supermarket.

There is a difference between expanding because customers need additional services and launching products simply because technology makes it easier to do so.

AI will undoubtedly make building products faster. But distribution, customer trust, regulatory permissions and access to financial networks are not going to become less important.

In fact, they could become the real differentiators.

And this brings me back to the original question. Are we adapting to the AI hype, or are we building businesses that will still make sense when the excitement settles?

I suspect we’ll see plenty of companies launch products that struggle to find a market. We’ll also see businesses use AI, stablecoins and new financial infrastructure to solve problems that have existed for years.

The two aren’t mutually exclusive.

I don’t think the future of fintech will necessarily belong to the companies building the most products or entering the most markets. It will belong to those that understand where the real opportunity sits and build the infrastructure to support it.

Because making money move is one thing.

Making it move globally, securely, efficiently and increasingly without human intervention is a very different proposition.

And that’s where I think the next big fintech opportunity lies.

title: Fed president pitches FedNow
snippet: Jeff Schmid, who leads the Kansas City Federal Reserve, nudged credit union executives last week to adopt faster payment options, like FedNow.
fullText:
The Federal Reserve has been trying to increase adoption of its FedNow instant payments system, and some regional Fed bank leaders are taking up the campaign.

Kansas City Federal Reserve Bank President Jeff Schmid addressed the issue in a speech last week at a National Credit Union Management Association conference. While he talked mainly about the economy, he devoted a significant chunk of the address to encouraging the credit union audience to consider adopting faster payment practices.

“Why do instant payments matter now?” he asked attendees, according to the text of his speech, delivered to the group in Hawaii on Nov. 15. “Because the market has changed.”

Today, 78% of consumers “prefer faster payments when given the option” and 66% of businesses “are likely to use instant payments if their financial institution offers them,” Schmid said, citing Fed research. 

Real-time payment systems, like FedNow, allow payments to move within seconds, as opposed to days for some legacy systems. FedNow is also available for use around the clock and on weekends. While that makes such systems more expedient to use, it also presents difficulties if an errant payment needs to be reversed.

Federal Reserve officials have been trying hard to persuade U.S. banks and credit unions to sign up for FedNow since it launched in July 2023, just weeks before Schmid took office the following month. The system is available only to financial institutions in the U.S.

FedNow adoption by financial institutions has been slow-going. In September, the Fed announced it would offer a discount on FedNow fees, starting Jan. 1, 2027, seemingly to spur more interest. Nonetheless, only those enrolled in certain Fed service programs and meeting specified FedNow volume thresholds, are eligible for reduced fees.

Currently, about 2,000 of the approximately 8,400 financial institutions in the U.S. are FedNow participants. That means only about a quarter of the ever-consolidating industry has signed up to be part of the Fed’s faster payments system over the past three years. 

That could be partly because the private sector had already created a real-time payments system in the form of the RTP network in 2017, giving it a first-mover advantage in attracting banks and credit unions. 

With RTP owned by The Clearing House, which is in turn owned by some of the largest banks in the world, FedNow was expected to have more appeal for smaller financial institutions that might not want to join a network owned by their larger rivals. 

How big banks use FedNow

Many of the major U.S. banks, including seven of the ten biggest, also participate in FedNow, giving them a back-up system for faster payments.

For instance, Capital One Financial isn’t interested in “picking a winner” between FedNow and RTP, but rather using both in case one system has a hiccup, said Capital One Managing Vice President Avik Chatterjee, who oversees payments at the bank. He has observed that other banks are doing the same, he said in an interview last month.

“What we want to strive for is, give the redundancy of real-time rails for our customers,” Chatterjee said. “We definitely want to participate on both the rails.”

While the big banks account for the majority of the volume that passes over FedNow, Schmid noted that smaller financial institutions – those with less than $10 billion in assets – make up 95% of FedNow participants.

Still, Schmid presented statistics that show credit unions aren’t necessarily keen to engage with FedNow. Only about 600 credit unions, of some 4,200 in the country, had joined FedNow as of the end of July, equal to about one in seven credit unions nationwide, he said.

“There is room to grow, but the momentum is real,” he observed. “Credit union participation is up more than 40% year-over-year.”  

He emphasized that more participation is important because the benefit of the system grows with more endpoints. “A payment network becomes more valuable with every institution that joins, and especially with every institution that can both send and receive,” Schmid said.

Use cases for instant payments that have been gaining ground over the past few years include quick payments to workers through earned wage access services. Also, because real-time systems operate around-the-clock, they are useful for the settlement of transactions that sometimes take place on weekends, like auto loans for the purchase of a car.

It makes sense for consumers and businesses to embrace faster payments, partly because such payments lower risks associated with slower settlement, especially for small businesses that crave price certainty, Schmid said.  “Faster access to funds improves liquidity for households and businesses,” he said.

However, of the financial institutions that have chosen to be a part of FedNow, many are hedging their risks by signing up just to receive real-time transactions, but not to send real-time payments. That means they can collect those payments without letting them flow out.

Using FedNow to counter fraud threats

The Kansas City Fed president painted a picture of instant payments being more insulated from fraud risks than some other forms of payment, namely paper checks. 

With that comment he was likely trying to counter a concern that banking and financial professionals have had since the advent of real-time payments: That faster payments would result in faster fraud. 

It’s an issue that Matt Clark, who is the chief revenue officer for business-to-business payments at the check and fintech company Deluxe, heard industry counterparts talking about earlier this month at the Association for Financial Professionals industry conference. While those professionals are eager to participate in faster payments, they’re balancing that desire with caution related to fraud, he said.

“We'll obviously continue to shift towards faster payments, but there is still that risk of increasing your fraud numbers by allowing that faster payment,” Clark said in an interview Thursday. 

Schmid urged the listeners in the audience to consider how they might “offer speed without sacrificing safety.” In addition to security tools built into FedNow that use historical data to spot problematic patterns in real-time, the system lets financial institutions control how they use the system, he said.

“On the sending side, you set your own limits, your own controls, and your own hours, based on what fits your members and your operational capacity,” Schmid said. “What you commit to is being ready to receive, around the clock, so that when someone sends your member money, it arrives.”

Further touting FedNow’s protections, he said the Fed is working with the private sector to keep improving FedNow’s risk management features.

“Efficient and safe payments are the circulatory system of the economy,” Schmid said. “When money flows reliably, other products and services can deliver their full value. When it doesn't, even the most thoughtful lending program or polished mobile app will be constrained.”

title: PayPal’s new CFO lands big pay
snippet: The digital payments player handed Claire Bramley, an HP alum, a $30 million pay package to take the chief financial officer post in February.
fullText:
Dive Brief:

Incoming PayPal CFO Claire Bramley is set to receive more than $30 million in stock awards and bonus compensation upon taking the top finance seat for the payments provider in February, according to a Friday regulatory filing. She will succeed Jamie Miller, who has served as PayPal’s CFO since 2023, and become CFO on Feb. 1, according to a Friday press release announcing the move.

PayPal is set to grant Bramley a one-time cash sign-on bonus of $5 million, payable in two installments contingent upon her continued employment with the company, according to the filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The company said it will also grant Bramley restricted stock units with a target grant value of $6 million, a sign-on RSU award with a value of $14 million, and a grant of performance-based RSUs with a grant date value of $6 million, according to the filing. In addition, Bramley’s compensation will include an annual base salary of $875,000, and she will be eligible to receive a target annual bonus of up to 125% of her base pay, according to the SEC filing.

Dive Insight:

The CFO transition is one of several executive moves announced Friday by the company, which in addition to its branded checkout service also owns and operates Venmo and Braintree.

Bramley will join fellow HP alum and PayPal CEO Enrique Lores at the San Jose, California-based company as it leans on a restructured leadership team as of this year to execute on a multi-year turnaround strategy.

Bramley is joining PayPal from financial software company Xero, where she has served as its CFO since June, according to her LinkedIn profile. Prior to Xero, which offers accounting software for small to midsize businesses, she served as CFO for Teradata. Her past experience also includes 14 years at technology company HP in roles such as global controller and finance leader for its Europe, Middle East and Africa division.

“What really attracted me to this role is the chance to help shape what’s next,” Bramley wrote in a Friday post on her LinkedIn profile announcing her move.” PayPal has played such an important role in transforming global commerce, and there’s so much more potential to unlock.”

Lores, formerly the CEO of HP, assumed PayPal’s top executive seat in March.

Since Lores took the seat, the payments provider has made numerous leadership transitions aimed at boosting profits and recovering consumer and investor attention. In April, he initiated the reorganization, with the company announcing it would be moving into a “simplified three business operating model,” according to a press release at the time. Those three areas include checkout Solutions & PayPal; consumer financial services & Venmo; and payment services & crypto.

On Friday, PayPal named Kartik Mani as its president and head of consumer financial services and Venmo; Suzan Kereere as president and head of payment services and crypto; and Juan Rio as executive vice president of AI business transformation and operations.

In another move, Brian Lee, formerly the chief risk officer for Goldman Sachs, joined the company’s board of directors — filling a vacancy created when it increased the size of its board from 11 to 12 members, PayPal said in a separate press release Friday.

The November appointments come after PayPal has “made significant progress in defining where we want to take PayPal and how we will compete and win,” Lores said in a statement included in the release.

“With our three-year strategies in place, our focus is now on execution,” he added. “These appointments bring together experienced leaders with the capabilities to accelerate innovation, strengthen our businesses and deliver greater value to our customers and shareholders.”

In its most recent earnings report Oct. 27, Lores touted PayPal’s progress but noted the company still has “more work to do.” The company reported increases in total payment volume and net revenue, according to its earnings release for the third quarter. Net income fell by about 14% year-over-year to about $1.1 billion, while earnings per diluted share inched down by 4% to $1.25.

Miller will step down from her current role as chief financial and operating officer effective as of Feb. 2 after a three-year tenure and a stint as its interim CEO in February — after then CEO and President Alex Chriss exited following an earnings miss and weak guidance, according to company filings and reports at the time.

Miller will receive severance payments and benefits applicable upon a termination without cause according to her separation agreement with the company, according to the Friday SEC filing.

PayPal will provide an update on its three-strategy progress during its fourth-quarter earnings report, the company said Friday.

title: How digital dollars improve cross-border payment management
snippet: As businesses look for more dependable ways to pay partners across borders, digital dollars are an emerging option.
fullText:
As businesses look for more dependable ways to pay suppliers and partners across borders, digital dollars — a form of internet-native money — are emerging as a practical option. 

Instead of hopping from bank to bank as each institution runs its own system, digital dollars allow money to move and settle on shared digital networks, just like how information moves across the internet. 

“Think of a digital dollar like an email,” said Meridith Perry, general manager of new business initiatives at Paystand. “It can be sent instantly and arrives within minutes. You see the status, so you know whether delivery failed or if it’s been opened. You can also attach information to it.”

With this infrastructure, senders and recipients access a shared payment record that details transaction amounts, send and receive dates and accompanying payment details so both sides can refer to that information whenever questions arise.

While adoption is early, finance teams that are putting digital dollars to work already report benefits, especially when it comes to cross-border payment operations. 

According to recent research from Paystand and CFO Dive’s Studio, financial leaders point to three ways digital dollars are improving international payments.

1. Payments Don’t Fail as Often

International payments moving along traditional rails pass through multiple banks and intermediary institutions, which makes failure hard to diagnose. This fragmentation puts finance teams at the mercy of updates that come from parties outside their control.

When an international payment fails or can’t be confirmed, the transaction can stall. This can cause 

Delays in critical business activities that depend on payments. While finance teams lose time on investigating settlement disputes and determining whether they need to resend funds, suppliers are left stalling as they await payment confirmation. 

When using digital dollars, however, 72% of users say fewer payments fail, are returned, or must be chased, research from Paystand and CFO Dive’s Studio found. Because they provide a direct, traceable record of payment with fewer handoffs, using digital dollars can mean less time spent tracking transactions and issuing repayments. This helps finance teams keep payments on track without manual follow-up.

2. Visibility into Payment Status Is Clearer 

To track a traditional international payment, status information is often split across sending banks, intermediary banks, receiving banks and payment providers. Once funds leave the sending bank, a  challenge arises. Finance teams often lack a direct, real-time view of an international payment’s progress. They have to ask their bank or the supplier for an update, which creates work. Those updates may arrive late or only during business hours, so they may already be out of date when the team receives them.

“The biggest challenge we hear about international payables is the lack of visibility or transparency,” Perry said. “This creates an operational-process burden: someone has to keep checking to see if payment arrived, or verify the payment amount.”

Because finance teams can’t tell where an international payment is in the process, suppliers, too, are in the dark as to when funds will arrive or if action needs to be taken to address a delay.

Digital-dollar users don’t have to piece together these updates as often: 56% report better visibility compared to previous payment methods, Paystand and CFO Dive’s Studio research found.

When using internet-native money, both parties use the shared record of activity created by the transaction to confirm whether a payment was sent, received or requires follow-up. This empowers finance teams to share updates with suppliers and stakeholders so both sides can plan around incoming funds and make sure problems don’t hold up other work.

“With traditional international payments, you may see two different numbers when you look at your bank compared to the other party’s bank,” Perry said. “But a shared transaction record gives both sides a common starting point: what moved, when it moved and whether the transfer was confirmed. When that record is connected to the invoice and accounting workflow, finance spends less time reconstructing what happened and can resolve exceptions sooner.”

3. Payments Are Completed Faster 

Slow payments can impact supplier relationships, time-sensitive purchases and access to funds, making it harder for businesses to secure the money they need and put it to work. And traditional cross-border payments are often held up due to factors like:

Bank cutoff times

Non-business days

Compliance reviews

Currency conversion

But nearly 1 in 3 respondents to the research from Paystand and CFO Dive’s Studio who use digital dollars say money arrives faster than with traditional payment methods. Digital-dollar networks operate continuously and often reduce the number of institutions involved in transactions. The result: Businesses can meet obligations on time and manage liquidity more responsively.

Perry pointed to a recent example.

“We worked with a business that held invoices for weeks to consolidate payments and pay one wire fee,” she said. “A more flexible payment process could let it pay sooner when that helps release an order. Payment timing should follow the needs of the business.”

The Cost of a Payment Is About More than Fees

“The transaction fee is only one part of the cost of a payment. Uncertainty creates work, ties up cash and delays decisions. The business case for digital dollars is whether they reduce those costs and give finance teams more control over when money becomes usable,” said Perry. “Digital dollars can reduce those demands.” 

Digital dollars give finance teams a clearer view of money in motion and more control over payment performance. For businesses that depend on suppliers and partners across borders, these benefits help keep payment issues from turning into business disruptions.

These follow demands it made for people to repay loans, or purported loans, provided as part of disguised remuneration schemes.

Disguised remuneration schemes saw people – often contractors, consultants and agency workers – paid for their work through loans instead of regular salaries. HMRC has published guidance for those affected.

Some of those affected dispute liability for the amounts being claimed and challenge whether the debts can be legally enforced. If they're unenforceable, borrowers cannot be forced to pay the money back or have any of their assets seized against the debt without a specific order.

Under the requirements we’ve agreed, Ethica:

Will write to affected consumers, explaining that they do not have an enforceable obligation to make payment at this stage. (This means they do not need to pay now while regulatory and legal issues relating to the purported loans are resolved.)

Will not make further demands for payment from affected consumers in the current proposed court claim while regulatory and legal issues are resolved.

Additionally, Ethica and West 28 will not ask a court to make a judgment against someone who has not responded to a legal claim. This is known as a ‘default judgment’.  

However, consumers should not ignore any formal court documents they receive on this issue. They should consider seeking independent legal or debt advice before deciding what to do.

Additional protections for vulnerable consumers are being put in place and Ethica will identify affected consumers who may be vulnerable.

It has not yet been decided whether the debts can be enforced, which may be decided by a court.  

The requirements agreed protect consumers from avoidable harm while the relevant regulatory and legal issues are resolved.  

Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.

title: Researchers spot ACH loopholes
snippet: University of Massachusetts academics have identified vulnerabilities that hackers could exploit in restricted bank accounts.
fullText:
Dive Brief:

Researchers at the University of Massachusetts have published a new study raising the alarm regarding cyberattacks fraudsters can use to target ACH bank transfers, the university said Monday.

The study, titled Credit Without Debit: Formal Verification of Banking Payment Systems, examined three new tactics hackers could have used to pilfer funds from unsuspecting banks and their customers, the university said.

The researchers alerted the at-risk banks to the problem and said the attacks have not been replicable since then. They presented their findings during the ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security on Monday, the university noted.

Dive Insight:

Researchers at the University of Massachusetts contended that hackers could exploit flaws in Nacha’s ACH transfer process. Nacha is the association that oversees the national automated clearing house for payments, setting rules and standards for bank-to-bank transfers.

Though Nacha’s operating rules allow financial institutions to authorize checks once and make provisional credit spendable before the other bank has determined whether to execute the debit transactions, the researchers found that this could result in available funds at one bank while the corresponding debit fails at the other bank. 

“Our goal is to strengthen financial security,” University of Massachusetts Amherst Professor Taqi Raza said in a press release. “The way we strengthen it is we find the loopholes and tell the banks, ‘okay, fix this problem.’”

Raza co-authored the study with Ali Malik, a doctoral candidate in electrical and computer science at the university.

The researchers identified three “credit-without-debit” attacks used by fraudsters and classified them into three threat categories they called: “creditbleed,” “creditmint” and “creditreset.” 

Creditbleed attacks involve initiating an ACH debit to a restricted account at another bank. Then, when the original bank fails to settle the bogus transaction, it will accumulate spendable funds for attackers to spend until the bank with the restricted account eventually reverses the transaction, the researchers said. 

When connecting a new external bank account, banks usually require account holders to enter the correct amount of change used for micro-deposits to verify their ownership. But attackers using the creditmint technique can trick banks into routing small deposits into restricted accounts that can’t send verification deposits back to the original bank, enabling fraudsters to repeatedly trigger those transactions and collect the spoils, the researchers explained in their study. 

In creditreset attacks, hackers use debit-restricted bank accounts to falsely pay credit card payments and increase the card’s credit line. When the card issuer tries to collect funds from the bank, the transaction fails, allowing fraudsters to spend more on a higher credit line, according to the study. 

The university declined to name which banks were affected by these disclosures, because “our work focuses on systematically identifying vulnerabilities in bank-to-bank transfers rather than individual institutions,” Raza said in an email. “The vulnerability disclosure to Nacha [is] handled through the banks; on checking, the reported issues appear to have been addressed in the updated Nacha specification.”

Nacha sees its accredited ACH professionals as mindful of the system’s parameters. They “are well versed in return risk – that an ACH debit can be returned for approximately two banking days for a number of reasons such as insufficient funds or frozen account,” a spokesperson for Nacha said by email. “Whether an originating bank or its ACH originating customer should allow funds from the debit to be withdrawn before the return deadline expires is their own call based on their own business needs and risk tolerances.”

UMass’ study comes as ACH payments have risen in popularity in recent years. In the third quarter, ACH Network payments jumped 5.9% year over year to 9.3 billion, according to an October Nacha press release. The value of those payments surged 10.2% from a year earlier to $25.6 trillion. 

Meanwhile, major payments providers are tracking and bracing themselves for fraud attempts. 

In its analysis of corporate and consumer fraud attacks released in May, Visa said it found roughly $1 billion in scam transactions in the second half of last year. Months later, the company acquired the cybersecurity and fraud-prevention company BioCatch for $2.4 billion to strengthen its anti-fraud offerings.

title: PayPal CEO remakes team
snippet: Chief Financial Officer Jamie Miller, who served as the digital payment company’s interim CEO at one point, will leave as CEO Enrique Lores installs new managers.
fullText:
PayPal Holdings installed a new set of top managers on Friday as the digital payments player announced its chief financial and operating officer, Jamie Miller, will leave the company.

The management shake-up comes as PayPal CEO Enrique Lores, who took the top post in March after serving on the company’s board, tries to jump-start profitable growth at the company. With two of his predecessors who faced the same challenge falling short, the company has had three CEOs in as many years.

Miller has seen the company through a series of executive changes and alterations to the PayPal’s strategic course since she joined the company three years ago. Lores acknowledged her contributions in a press release announcing a series of executive appointments on Friday. Miller will remain in her role until Feb. 1, according to a filing the company made Friday with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

“Miller has guided the company through a period of extraordinary change, including leading through a CEO transition and playing an instrumental role in defining the new strategy,” the release said.

PayPal has struggled to meet growth goals in recent years as it faced increasingly fierce competition from a slew of fintech startups advancing the digital payments tools it ushered into initial use almost three decades ago. With the advent of artificial intelligence and cryptocurrencies, new entrants are further updating payments tools and the options for digitized payments.

The company reportedly passed up the opportunity to sell the business to digital rival Stripe and an investment firm partner. Instead, Lores has opted to restructure the company’s divisions, shed thousands of workers and divest parts of the business. He has also emphasized a strategy to sell more financial services to consumers.

Miller will be replaced as CFO by Claire Bramley, who has held the same role at the small business accounting and payments software company Xero since April 2025. That company has expanded at a rapid pace, including with the acquisition of the bill-pay company Melio in June.

In addition, PayPal announced that Chief Risk Officer Aaron Webster will exit and the company’s senior vice president of credit and fraud risk, Ratinder Bedi, will become the interim head of the risk organization while the company searches for a permanent replacement.

San Jose, California-based PayPal also appointed a number of other top executives, in some cases superseding other appointments that Lores made shortly after he became CEO.

The company named Kartik Mani as president and head of consumer financial services and its peer-to-peer business Venmo. He comes to PayPal from American Express, where he was president of global network and partner services, according to the release.

Alexis Sowa, who was tapped in April as interim lead for the consumer financial services and Venmo business unit, will continue as general manger of Venmo, reporting to Mani.

Suzan Kereere was promoted to the role of president and head of payment services and crypto, moving up from her post leading the company’s global markets strategy. Kereere will replace Jeff Pomeroy, who was interim lead for payment services and crypto business, in another instance of Lores refining his team approach. Pomeroy will report to Kereere.

The company also named Juan Rio as executive vice president of AI business transformation and operations. He will join the company at the end of this month from the consulting firm Brightstar.AI, where he was a managing director. 

Frank Keller, who was named president of the PayPal branded business in April, will still oversee that area, including checkout solutions.

Alongside the changes, the company also said a new director, former Goldman Sachs chief risk officer, Brian J. Lee, had joined the board. 

Miller became PayPal’s CFO in November 2023, and was elevated to take on the additional operating chief duties in February of last year under then-CEO Alex Chriss, who left the company earlier this year. After Chriss exited, she was interim CEO for a period in February before Lores took the role.

“In connection with Ms. Miller’s departure, the Company and Ms. Miller entered into a separation and release agreement on November 19, 2026, which provides that Ms. Miller will be eligible to receive the severance payments and benefits applicable upon a termination without cause,” the company said in the SEC filing. 

The filing also noted that there were no disputes between Miller and the company related to the financial results.

title: Travel brands aren’t the only ones that benefit from non-prime credit card partnerships
snippet: 75% of non-prime consumers plan to travel. Here's how brands can earn their loyalty.
fullText:
Travel continues to remain one of the most important experiences that consumers are not willing to pass up — even non-prime credit consumers. In fact, seventy-five percent of non-prime consumers plan to take a trip this year, but only 20% have booked, according to a Concora Credit Travel Intent Survey. However, financial issues such as inflation, tariffs, and higher airplane prices continue to give consumers pause.

For the non-prime consumer, travel is not a luxury. Non-prime consumers are usually intentional, budget-conscious, and deliberate; they are often working adults in the middle of raising a family, with 40% of those surveyed indicating full-time employment status. They view travel as a much-needed break from hard work, and a way to stay connected with family and friends. (68% of respondents reported that their main reason for travel was vacation or leisure, while 64% of respondents mentioned visiting family or friends). Most trips are domestic and short with over half of surveyed travelers booking a 2 to 3 night stay, and 66% staying within the U.S., while 49% of respondents plan on driving to their travel destination.

Surprise costs kill bookings

Even with the general perspective of travel as a non-negotiable, what stands in the way of non-prime consumers fully booking a trip is not a change of heart or loss of interest, but rather, cost. Cost is the lead reason for abandoned carts: 55% of non-prime consumers said the top reason to abandon a booking was that total costs were higher than expected, while 39% cited late-appearing fees. So how can travel brands convert the middle ground of 55% of non-prime consumers who are “still planning a trip without having booked?”

The answer: connecting with a credit card partnership. If a consumer knows they can pay off a trip over time, the idea of travel is no longer unattainable — it becomes something tangible that they can reasonably afford. When travel brands partner with credit card offerings such as Concora Credit, a financial services company and credit servicer that provides credit card and financing programs tailored for non-prime consumers, the goal is not about promising unaffordable, out-of-budget range trips for consumers just to increase bottom lines. 

According to Rolando De Gracia, chief commercial officer of Concora Credit, the partnership is actually about “helping to make a trip that already fits the budget become manageable, with terms that are clear from the start.” Non-prime credit card partnerships can help:

Clearly outline travel and payment terms from the beginning of the booking process

Eliminate surprise fees that lead to cart abandonment later on

Increase credit card approval rates, which directly correlate to booking completions

In fact, 6% of non-prime consumers would abandon a booking after being turned down by a credit card. According to 55% of those surveyed, the lowest total price is the most important factor when it comes to deciding how and when to book a trip, while 38% of respondents said that no hidden fees was the most important. And it’s not that non-prime users wouldn’t take the trip — they just pivot. As De Gracia explains, “Our survey data suggest that when money gets tight, these travelers don’t necessarily give up the trip. They adjust it. They go closer to home, take a shorter trip, or choose less expensive lodging. They trade down how they travel.” Credit card partners can help meet their non-prime consumers where they are with their travel and budget wishlist, while ensuring that the trip is still within their price point.

Credit card partnerships benefit both brand and consumer

Connecting with Concora Credit helps both travel brands and consumers. For travel brands, it’s an opportunity to tap into an underutilized market. For consumers, both building credit and taking those non-negotiable trips become a reality. 

And while many non-prime consumers do book directly with a travel provider, travel site partnerships such as Expedia.com or Booking.com remain an important and major player in how non-prime consumers complete their bookings. Over 27% of respondents to the Concora Credit Travel Intent Survey said that they typically book their personal travel with online travel agencies. 

Regardless of how they book, “the bottom line is that the trip becomes more achievable. A credit card lets travelers spread the cost over time instead of drawing down the cash in their checking account all at once,” says De Gracia.

According to the Concora Credit Travel Intent Survey, only 36% of non-prime travelers expect to use a credit card to book their trips, with many instead planning to pay upfront using debit cards or funds from their checking or savings accounts. However, cardholders who are approved for credit through credit-travel partnerships may be more inclined to use credit cards for their travel purchases. In fact, when asked what would make a trip more accessible, 33% of respondents cited “paying over time through a payment plan.” What’s more, credit card options provide non-prime consumers with more opportunities to book directly with airlines and hotels, helping foster repeat bookings and longer-term customer loyalty.

title: M&T aims to ‘dial up’ credit card rewards
snippet: The regional lender is looking to offer simple and easy-to-understand credit card perks, in line with recent customer feedback.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                

The regional lender is looking to offer simple and easy-to-understand credit card perks, in line with recent customer feedback.

        

            

        Published Nov. 19, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                An M&T Bank branch in the Brooklyn borough of New York City on April 17, 2024. The bank is changing card rewards to better meet consumer preferences.
            
        
            Spencer Platt via Getty Images
        
    
    
    

 
    

First published on

    

    

                    

M&T customers want simpler, easier-to-use credit card rewards, and the regional bank is working to meet those preferences amid an intensely competitive landscape.

That’s according to Chris Nichols, the Buffalo, New York-based lender’s head of retail banking, who said the bank’s recent credit card enhancements “acknowledge[d] an opportunity to dial it up a little bit.”

Earlier this month, $218.9 billion-asset M&T updated the rewards structure for one of its credit cards, bolstering rewards on grocery and gas purchases for cardholders. The cards continue to come with flexible redemption options and no annual fee.

“One of the things that's core to M&T and our strategy is really focusing on being the primary banking relationship for our customers,” Nichols said in a recent interview. “To do that, we’ve got to be able to meet all of their needs,” including with a competitive credit card.

M&T brought its credit card program in-house in 2010, having previously turned to a partner. The bank has four credit cards that it pitches to existing customers. “It’s not a product that we lead with for non-customers,” Nichols said.

The lender has about $6.8 billion in credit card commitments; M&T doesn’t break out outstanding card balances or the number of card accounts, a spokesperson said. Card revenue in the third quarter was $90 million, which was about the same as in the year-ago period.  

The bank declined to share a growth target for the credit card business or how much it’s invested in recent enhancements, other than to say it’s making “strategic investments” to deliver what customers are looking for.

M&T routinely evaluates its products to ensure they’re still meeting customer needs. Recent feedback indicated bank customers desired simple and easy-to-understand credit card rewards anchored to their everyday spending, Nichols said. 

“If we believe we’ve got a right to get our customers to switch from their current credit card provider to ours, we’ve got to make sure we’ve got that compelling value proposition,” he said. “We know our customers have a lot of options.”

“The players are becoming more and more prevalent, and in some cases disruptive,” Nichols said, referring to fintechs and nonbanks providing brands and retailers with embedded credit programs. “So we've got to make sure we're upping our game on that: What's the value to our customers to go along with the people and the brand that we bring?”

fullText:
Credit cards are a useful financial tool for many – offering flexibility and helping people manage spending and cash flow.

But if customers only make low repayments over a long period, they can end up in debt for years while racking up interest and charges. 

The persistent debt rules we introduced in 2018 aimed to tackle this.

They said that lenders had to identify customers who, over an 18-month period, paid more in interest, fees and charges than towards their balance.

Lenders had to contact these customers and encourage them to increase repayments if they could afford it, and if they were still struggling, lenders had to take additional steps to help them repay their balances sustainably.

What changed for consumers

Our evaluation shows that consumer outcomes improved between 2018 and early 2023.  

Percentage of accounts in persistent debt

          

            						

We found that the proportion of credit card accounts in persistent debt fell by more than half between 2018 and early 2023, from 7% to 3%. Over the same period, monthly interest and fees for customers in persistent debt also fell.

Importantly, we found that many consumers changed their repayment behaviour after their provider contacted them.

In the 6 months after receiving their first persistent debt letter, over half of these customers raised their average repayments, around two-thirds reduced their average debt, and a majority reduced the proportion of their available credit they were using.

We also found that many customers moved out of persistent debt altogether. Of those who received an initial letter, more than half had left persistent debt within 18 months of receiving it, rising to almost two-thirds within 27 months.

These are encouraging signs. They suggest that clear communications and timely interventions can help those consumers who can afford to pay down their debt more quickly.

Supporting consumers who are struggling

However, these rules on their own can’t help all customers who may be really struggling.

Some simply aren’t able to pay more. Lenders need to do more than send communications: the earlier intervention rules we introduced at the same time as the persistent debt rules require firms to support consumers if they see signs of financial difficulty. The Consumer Duty also requires firms to act to prevent foreseeable harm.

Firms must understand their customers’ individual circumstances, communicate with them clearly and provide support such as reducing interest, fees or charges and directing people to free debt advice.

Our evaluation highlights the complexity of assessing outcomes in a changing economic environment.

The period covered by the research included the Covid-19 pandemic, the cost of living crisis, rising interest rates, and wider regulatory and market developments.  

So, although this means we can’t conclude that the persistent debt rules alone caused the improvements we observed, the consistency of the findings suggest the overall direction was positive in the period covered by our review.

Going forward, the new comprehensive data we collect from firms (product sales data) will help us to monitor the consumer credit market, including levels of persistent debt, and how changing economic conditions are affecting it.  

Credit card use and defaults have increased since the period covered by the evaluation. Initial analysis of recent product sales data suggests rates of persistent debt have risen, although it is still below the level it was at when we introduced the rules.

Help at the right time

One of the priorities in our strategy is helping consumers navigate their financial lives. To make this happen, firms need to ensure consumers receive good outcomes. Firms must support customers effectively, particularly when they are vulnerable or experiencing financial difficulty.

This evaluation suggests that the persistent debt framework can be an important part of achieving that goal.

There’s more to do. As household costs continue to rise, we’ll continue to monitor how firms support customers in persistent debt and ensure that those struggling with repayments receive the help they need at the right time.

Reducing persistent debt is not just about lowering balances and reducing the length of time it takes to pay off debt. It’s about helping consumers achieve better financial outcomes and become more financially resilient in the long term.

The new law gives merchants a legal basis for rounding retail cash transactions as pennies disappear.

        

            

        Published Nov. 23, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                President Donald Trump signed legislation on November 20, 2026 that formally ends U.S. penny production and offers merchants a framework for rounding cash transactions.
            
        
            Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

President Donald Trump signed the Common Cents Act into law on Friday, offering merchants a legal framework for rounding to the nearest nickel as the U.S. penny supply gradually dwindles.

The law – a top legislative priority for merchant trade groups – also formally ends production of the 1-cent coin, although the government stopped making it last year. Additionally, the measure authorizes the Treasury Department to research zinc as a copper replacement in the nickel to lower that coin’s 13-cent production cost.

With the law, “restaurant operators can have the confidence that they are handling cash transactions in a way that works for their business and for their customers,” Sean Kennedy, chief advocacy officer of the National Restaurant Association, said in a statement Friday. About 25% of restaurant purchases are still made with cash, Kennedy said.

Dive Insight:

The U.S. Mint announced in November 2025 that it had struck its final batch of pennies, nine months after Trump directed the U.S. Treasury to stop making the coin, citing their cost inefficiency. The department estimated $56 million in savings by ending penny production. 

Under the law, transactions that end with 1, 2, 6 or 7 cents would be rounded down to the nearest amount divisible by five; those ending with 3, 4, 8 or 9 cents in the sum are rounded up. Electronic transactions are excluded. 

Rep. Lisa McClain, a Michigan Republican who co-sponsored the House version with Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia of California, celebrated the signing Friday with a post on the social media site X. 

The legislation had two votes in both the House and Senate earlier this year due to an amendment added in the Senate version when that chamber endorsed the bill in August. The House passed the bill a second time on Sept. 14, followed by the Senate two weeks later.

“Washington was spending nearly four cents to make every one-cent penny,” wrote McClain, who is chair of the House Republican Caucus. “Not anymore. That’s what common sense, and Common Cents, looks like.”

The National Grocers Association hailed the new law as a solution for a problem its supermarket members confront daily.

“Independent grocers process millions of transactions every day, and the disappearance of the penny created a very practical problem at the checkout counter,” Stephanie Johnson, the association’s senior vice president and head of government affairs, said in a Friday press release. The law “provides the clarity and legal protections retailers need to handle cash transactions consistently and fairly.”

The Senate version of the legislation was co-sponsored by Cynthia Lummis, a Wyoming Republican, and Kirsten Gillibrand, a Democrat from New York.

“This is a Main Street issue, and there was unanimous agreement in both chambers on the final bill,” Brennan Duckett, director of regulatory and policy for NACS, the National Association of Convenience Stores, said in a press release. “It’s a good feeling knowing that this law removes a few of the hurdles that retailers face every day, and that we helped solve a real-world problem.”

fullText:
How many of us read the terms and conditions of a contract before buying a financial product?

Contracts hold the detail that shapes everyone's financial life, whether you're taking out a loan, insuring your holiday, or signing up for a crypto wallet.

All firms are responsible for making sure that terms in their consumer contracts comply with the fairness and transparency requirements of the Consumer Rights Act (CRA) 2015. When those terms don’t comply, our Consumer Contracts team has powers to challenge firms directly.

This work shows how we use the full range of powers Parliament has given us, not only those in financial services legislation, to tackle harm.

Here's why it matters: if a term is found to be unfair, it's not just unenforceable – consumers may be due redress too. That's why it pays for firms to get this right from the start.

We review contract terms identified through our supervision of firms, information on social media, and referrals from consumers and other external stakeholders.  

When we take action  

We consider our rules and guidance, including the Consumer Duty, when deciding whether to act and which of our regulatory tools to use.  

Where we raise concerns about the fairness or transparency of terms, we expect firms to:  

Amend or delete the relevant terms so that the contract is fair and transparent, and stop relying on those terms in existing contracts.

Pay redress to consumers if the firm’s use of the terms has caused harm; and

In some cases, give us a voluntary undertaking under the CRA.  

Where necessary, we can apply for a court injunction to prevent a firm from using or enforcing the term against its customers. We can also seek a court order requiring it to pay redress.  

Examples of cases we've tackled

A crypto firm agreed to stop charging excessive storage fees which, in some cases, could exceed £40,000 a year. We intervened after finding it had charged inactive customers a disproportionate amount. The firm removed the term and paid redress to affected consumers.

A financial adviser updated its contracts after trying to charge a customer £800 for time spent handling a complaint. The charge was included in its terms and conditions, but we considered the term unfair because it could put people off making legitimate complaints. We also considered it inconsistent with the Consumer Duty and our own rules.

A travel insurer clarified unclear terms about what counted as a 12-hour delay and paid out £18,000 in redress to customers whose claims had been wrongly denied. Here, ambiguous wording was the problem, so we pushed for clearer terms that told consumers exactly what they were entitled to.

A lender improved the terms of a new credit product to give clearer information on costs and cancellation rights after we raised concerns ahead of launch. This is a good example of intervening early, through the authorisations process, to prevent unfair terms making it to market in the first place.

What we expect of firms

Firms should regularly check that their consumer contracts are fair, clear and transparent, and that they're being used fairly in practice.  

In practice, that means:

Taking into account consumers’ legitimate interests when designing contracts.

Using plain language, so customers understand what they're agreeing to: for example, what they might have to pay and what rights they have. Nobody should need a law degree to understand what they're signing up to.  

Avoiding surprises, by making important terms – fees, cancellation rights, variations, exclusions, complaints – easy to spot.

Reviewing contracts regularly to stay compliant with the latest requirements, rulings and judgments, and to learn from complaints, claims, cancellations, fees, customer outcomes and other data.

Testing whether customers actually understand key terms – not just assuming they do.

Improving staff training to ensure staff meet the standards set out in product literature, including contracts. Using complaints data to identify potentially unfair or unclear contract terms and make appropriate changes.

How to report concerns about unfair or unclear terms to us

Concerned about an unfair or unclear term in a financial services firm’s consumer contract? You can report it to us using our form. We can't always tell you what action we've taken, but, we can assure you, every report we receive gets considered.
